###### Abstract

Recent advances in large language models have enabled agentic systems
that automate machine learning pipeline construction from minimal user
input. However, existing agentic AutoML methods either depend on rigid
templates that limit adaptability, target narrow task domains, or rely
on free-form code generation that lacks reliability guarantees, leaving
intermediate errors to propagate silently and degrade the final model.
We present EvoML, an agentic framework for end-to-end ML pipeline
synthesis built on expert-grounded skills that evolve across runs,
executed through a validation-gated harness. The framework decomposes
pipeline construction into four phases coordinated by three agents: an
Orchestrator that enforces validation gates, advancing each phase only
when its outputs pass structural, execution, and semantic checks, which
precludes error propagation and keeps every artifact auditable; an
Executor that runs expert-grounded skills, grounded in the nnU-Net
workflow and pairing reusable templates with online adaptation; and a
Curator that performs post-run evolution, consolidating the scripts and
guidance recovered during a run into the skill library so it improves
across datasets. We evaluate EvoML on eight datasets spanning six
sophisticated, real-world ML task types, against agentic AutoML systems
and command-line coding tools. EvoML achieves full automation and the
best final model quality on all eight, spanning segmentation (up to 0.94
Dice), classification (0.99 accuracy), reconstruction (0.95 SSIM), and
denoising (0.79 normalized PSNR), while transferring to broader ML
tasks.

###### Index Terms: 

Automated Machine Learning, Multi-Agent Framework, Program Synthesis

## I Introduction

Automated Machine Learning (AutoML) aims to reduce the manual effort of
building ML solutions by automating stages such as data preparation,
model selection, hyperparameter optimisation, and pipeline
construction \[[1](#bib.bib13), [2](#bib.bib15)\]. Traditional systems
search over predefined model families, operators, and hyperparameter
spaces \[[3](#bib.bib17), [4](#bib.bib18), [5](#bib.bib16)\], but their
fixed search spaces and hand-designed primitives limit flexibility for
complex workflows, domain-specific processing, or end-to-end executable
code \[[6](#bib.bib19), [7](#bib.bib20), [8](#bib.bib21)\]. Large
language models (LLMs) and agentic coding systems offer a new
opportunity to interpret high-level intent, generate executable code,
invoke tools, and iteratively refine solutions \[[9](#bib.bib14)\].
Building on these capabilities, recent work applies LLMs to individual
ML pipeline stages, including data and feature
extraction \[[10](#bib.bib23), [11](#bib.bib24), [12](#bib.bib25)\],
model selection and training \[[13](#bib.bib26)\], \[[14](#bib.bib22)\],
and hyperparameter optimisation \[[15](#bib.bib27)\],
\[[16](#bib.bib28)\], offering more flexible, context-aware automation
than fixed search spaces.

This potential has further motivated agentic AutoML systems that aim to
coordinate multiple ML stages within a single end-to-end workflow.
Recent systems \[[17](#bib.bib1), [18](#bib.bib2), [19](#bib.bib29)\]
demonstrate the potential of LLM-based agents for automating ML
workflows, but several limitations remain when applied to robust
end-to-end pipeline construction. First, they often require users to
supply template code, dataset-specific features, or detailed solution
descriptions beyond minimal problem input, making automation sensitive
to the quality of human guidance. Second, execution is not consistently
governed by effective validation gates that verify whether each stage
has produced executable, reusable artifacts before subsequent stages
proceed; as a result, failures can propagate through the workflow,
leading to incomplete artifacts or requiring manual intervention to
diagnose and correct. Third, pipeline construction is commonly driven by
search over predefined operators, retrieved knowledge, or online
examples, which can limit robustness when tasks demand domain-specific
procedures or tight coordination across dependent stages. Finally,
failures observed during execution are rarely converted into persistent
improvements of the underlying procedures, leaving the system unable to
accumulate operational experience across runs.

To address these limitations, we propose EvoML, a validation-gated ML
pipeline synthesis framework with expert-grounded, self-evolving skills.
EvoML decomposes end-to-end pipeline synthesis into three coordinated
GPT-5.5 \[[20](#bib.bib59)\] agents. The Orchestrator governs
stage-by-stage progression through the ML workflow, enforcing
validation-gated transitions, advancing only when expected artifacts and
validation signals satisfy predefined criteria, such as successful
execution, required file generation, valid data format, or task-relevant
metric constraints, and triggering retries. The Executor performs each
stage by invoking reusable, expert-grounded skills, each of which
encodes a standard operating procedure for a specific ML stage,
including data preparation, model configuration, training,
hyperparameter optimisation, and code integration. The Curator analyses
validation and retry traces after each run, identifies skills that incur
repeated failures or excessive retries, and evolves those skills for
future executions, allowing the framework to continuously refine its
execution capabilities. By separating workflow control, skill-based
execution, and post-run skill evolution into distinct agent
responsibilities, the framework supports autonomous pipeline synthesis
from minimal user input while maintaining auditable validation, bounded
failure recovery, and continuous improvement.

This paper makes the following contributions.

- •
  We present a fully automated agentic system for ML pipeline synthesis
  that autonomously executes, monitors, and refines pipelines from
  minimal user input, without relying on task-specific templates or
  human guidance.
- •
  We introduce a unified validation-gated execution harness in which
  stage progression is governed by artifact- and metric-based checks,
  enabling robust transitions, bounded failure recovery, and auditable
  execution traces.
- •
  We couple expert-grounded skills with post-run evolution to support
  reliable and continuously improving ML pipeline synthesis,
  consolidating successful recoveries from validation and retry traces
  into persistent skill updates across runs.

The remainder of this paper is organised as follows:
Section [II](#S2 "II Background ‣ Validation-Gated ML Pipeline Synthesis with Expert-Grounded Self-Evolving Skills")
reviews previous methods on LLM-based program synthesis and agentic
AutoML.
Section [III](#S3 "III Methodology ‣ Validation-Gated ML Pipeline Synthesis with Expert-Grounded Self-Evolving Skills")
presents the EvoML framework, detailing its three-agent design,
expert-grounded skill library, validation-gated execution, and post-run
skill evolution.
Section [IV](#S4 "IV Evaluation ‣ Validation-Gated ML Pipeline Synthesis with Expert-Grounded Self-Evolving Skills")
reports the experimental evaluation across a range of ML tasks,
including ablation studies of the core components.
Section [V](#S5 "V Discussion ‣ Validation-Gated ML Pipeline Synthesis with Expert-Grounded Self-Evolving Skills")
provides an architectural comparison with the baselines and discusses
cost-efficiency and threats to validity.
Section [VI](#S6 "VI Conclusion ‣ Validation-Gated ML Pipeline Synthesis with Expert-Grounded Self-Evolving Skills")
concludes with a summary and future research directions.

## II Background

LLM-Based Program Synthesis Frameworks. Program synthesis, the automatic
generation of programs from high-level specifications, is a
long-standing software-engineering task \[[21](#bib.bib4)\]; early
formal, deductive approaches were limited in scalability and
generality \[[22](#bib.bib3)\]. Large language models trained on code
have since enabled the generation of syntactically correct, functionally
plausible code from natural language \[[23](#bib.bib5), [24](#bib.bib6),
[25](#bib.bib8), [26](#bib.bib7)\], and agentic coding frameworks extend
single-shot generation toward iterative, tool-augmented
workflows \[[27](#bib.bib9)\], \[[28](#bib.bib10)\]. Multi-agent systems
such as MetaGPT \[[29](#bib.bib31)\], ChatDev \[[30](#bib.bib32)\],
SWE-agent \[[31](#bib.bib30)\], and MaCTG \[[32](#bib.bib33)\] decompose
complex tasks across collaborating agents, and assistants such as GitHub
Copilot \[[33](#bib.bib37)\], Cursor \[[34](#bib.bib36)\],
Codex \[[35](#bib.bib34)\], and Claude Code \[[36](#bib.bib35)\] bring
these capabilities into practical use. These general-purpose frameworks,
however, are not designed for the structural and procedural demands of
ML pipeline construction: they lack domain-specific workflow
coordination and depend on human-supplied guidance, such as task
descriptions, template code, or annotated examples, limiting their
applicability to autonomous end-to-end synthesis.

Agentic AutoML Methods. Applying agentic coding to ML pipeline synthesis
raises challenges of stage coordination, domain-specific procedures, and
execution reliability. Early efforts addressed individual stages in
isolation: CAAFE \[[37](#bib.bib38)\] automates feature engineering and
DS-Agent \[[38](#bib.bib39)\] applies case-based reasoning to data
processing and training, but both rely on structured human input and
leave cross-stage coordination unaddressed.
AutoML-GPT \[[39](#bib.bib40)\] and SELA \[[40](#bib.bib41)\] attempt
end-to-end automation through LLM-generated pipelines and tree search,
yet still depend on detailed human input and lack validation-gated
progression or failure recovery. The most capable end-to-end systems are
AutoML-Agent \[[17](#bib.bib1)\], which coordinates multiple agents but
requires user-supplied task templates; M3Builder \[[19](#bib.bib29)\],
which performs strongly on medical imaging but is constrained to
specific dataset types and tasks; and MLZero \[[18](#bib.bib2)\], which
runs without manual input via documentation retrieval and iterative
debugging but validates only execution success and retains memory within
a single task. Across all of them, a common gap persists: none converts
execution-time failures into persistent improvements, leaving the system
unable to accumulate experience across runs.

## III Methodology

EvoML synthesises a complete, executable ML pipeline from a dataset and
a minimal task description, without task-specific templates or human
guidance. We follow a design-and-evaluate process in which the
limitations identified in Sections
[I](#S1 "I Introduction ‣ Validation-Gated ML Pipeline Synthesis with Expert-Grounded Self-Evolving Skills")–[II](#S2 "II Background ‣ Validation-Gated ML Pipeline Synthesis with Expert-Grounded Self-Evolving Skills")
are translated into three design requirements for reliable agentic ML
pipeline synthesis: preventing error propagation across stages,
grounding execution in reliable domain procedures, and retaining
successful recovery experience across runs. These requirements motivate
EvoML’s three core mechanisms: validation-gated orchestration,
expert-grounded skill execution, and post-run skill evolution.

Accordingly, Section
[III](#S3 "III Methodology ‣ Validation-Gated ML Pipeline Synthesis with Expert-Grounded Self-Evolving Skills")
first presents the overall system architecture and its three constituent
agents, then introduces the expert-grounded skill library, describes the
validation-gated execution that governs phase progression, and finally
presents the post-run evolution mechanism that refines the skill library
across runs.

### III-A System Overview

![Refer to caption](2611.04180v1/worflow_new.png)

Fig. 1: Overview of the proposed validation-gated agentic ML pipeline
synthesis framework. The Orchestrator progresses through four phases and
invokes the corresponding Executor skill group in sequence: Task
Understanding (skills 1–2), Planning (3–4), Training (5–7), and
Post-train Processing (8–9). After each phase, generated artifacts and
execution evidence are returned for gated validation; passed phases
advance, while failed phases trigger recovery. The Curator operates
after the run to evolve the skill library from accumulated execution
evidence.

Figure [1](#S3.F1 "Fig. 1 ‣ III-A System Overview ‣ III Methodology ‣ Validation-Gated ML Pipeline Synthesis with Expert-Grounded Self-Evolving Skills")
illustrates how the proposed framework addresses the ML pipeline
synthesis task through three dedicated agents: (1) the Orchestrator,
which governs synthesis progression through validation gates; (2) the
Executor, which runs expert-grounded skill groups from the skill library
for each phase; and (3) the Curator, which operates post-run, auditing
and evolving the skill library. For an ML pipeline synthesis task, the
input consists of a dataset and a minimal task description specifying
the task type and data path. Given this, the system autonomously
generates a complete, executable ML pipeline covering all stages from
data preparation to model training and evaluation. EvoML organises the
synthesis via these three coordinated agents across four main phases.

At runtime, the Orchestrator interprets the user request and drives the
four phases in turn, invoking the Executor with the corresponding skill
group at each: Task Understanding (dataset preparation and fingerprint
extraction), Planning (experiment planning and preprocessing), Training
(HPO based on Optuna \[[41](#bib.bib43)\], promotion, and full
training), and Post-Train Processing (evaluation aggregation and
artifact export). After each phase the Executor returns its artifacts
and logs for gate evaluation; on failure the Orchestrator returns the
failure context for a bounded retry, and on success it advances. Once
the run concludes, the Curator inspects the accumulated evidence,
identifies underperforming skills, and proposes verified updates to the
library for future runs.

This separation of concerns gives each agent an isolated context and
clear accountability at each phase boundary: the Orchestrator validates
independently of the code that produced the artifacts, the Executor
focuses solely on running skills, and the Curator analyses the complete
execution evidence post-run rather than reacting with partial context
mid-run. The four-phase structure mirrors the natural decomposition of
an ML pipeline, with validation boundaries that localise failures before
downstream computation is committed.

### III-B Expert-Grounded Skill Library Design

#### III-B1 Skill Structure and Expert Grounding

Following the Agent Skills format \[[42](#bib.bib45)\], each skill in
EvoML is a self-contained module comprising a Markdown specification, a
set of Python script templates, and a reference document that encodes
the relevant domain knowledge. The Markdown file encodes the stage
objective, expected inputs, the usage of the accompanying Python
templates, and a self-validation instruction for the Executor to verify
successful execution. The reference document, predominantly an
output-format specification such as the expected dataset format, grounds
each skill’s execution in a verifiable contract. Together, all skills
form a shared library from which the Executor is prompted to invoke the
appropriate skill at each stage of the current workflow.

Reliable end-to-end synthesis requires more than free-form code
generation; it demands a principled procedure. We therefore ground
EvoML’s skills in nnU-Net \[[43](#bib.bib44)\], a self-configuring
framework that achieves strong performance not through elaborate
architectures but by analysing the dataset and adapting preprocessing,
model, and training configuration to its characteristics. This
data-driven, configuration-first approach is not specific to any one
task type, which makes it a sound basis for general pipeline synthesis.
This grounding also resolves a fundamental tension in agentic synthesis:
pure LLM generation is flexible but structurally variable and unreliable
across runs, whereas fixed templates are consistent but cannot capture
task-specific requirements. Deriving templates from nnU-Net’s
well-defined procedures supplies structural consistency, while
LLM-generated adaptations retain the flexibility each task demands.
nnU-Net itself, however, requires manual deployment and expert
configuration per task and lacks automated validation; EvoML resolves
these limitations by encoding its workflow as agent-executable skills,
automating configuration while adding validation-gated execution and
cross-run evolution that nnU-Net lacks.

#### III-B2 Skill Library Composition

The library comprises nine skills spanning the four phases. The Dataset
preparation skill converts a raw dataset into the standardised nnU-Net
format, automatically selecting, cloning, and adapting the appropriate
converter for the input layout. The Fingerprint extraction skill then
computes a compact statistical summary of the dataset, including image
shape, voxel spacing, and intensity distribution, which conditions all
subsequent configuration decisions. From this fingerprint, the
Experiment planning skill derives the model and training configuration,
including network topology, patch size, and batch size, while the
Preprocessing skill crops, resamples to the target spacing, and
normalises intensities to produce training-ready arrays. The Optuna HPO
and HPO promotion skills are introduced beyond nnU-Net’s native workflow
to improve final performance. The HPO skill runs hyperparameter
optimisation trials on a fixed tuning fold, sampling learning rate,
weight decay, and early-stopping configurations, while the promotion
skill compares the best trial against the baseline configuration and
promotes it only when the performance gain exceeds a predefined
threshold. The Full training skill then executes the standard nnU-Net
five-fold cross-validation under the promoted configuration, augmented
with an early-stopping mechanism that halts training once validation
performance converges, and the Evaluation aggregation skill consolidates
the cross-validation predictions, determines postprocessing, and
computes the final metrics. Finally, the Artifact export skill packages
the executed stage scripts into a standalone, runnable pipeline. These
nine skills constitute a fixed, complete decomposition of the ML
pipeline; evolution therefore refines existing skills rather than
inserting or deleting them.

### III-C Validation-Gated Pipeline Execution

The Orchestrator and Executor interact in a structured
invoke-validate-advance loop within a unified validation-gated harness
that enforces phase-level contracts, manages artifact dependencies, and
provides bounded failure recovery across four phases from Task
Understanding to Post-Train Processing.

#### III-C1 Phase Execution

At each phase $`p_{k}`$, the Orchestrator invokes the Executor to run
the skill group $`\Phi_{k}`$, which takes the artifact set
$`\mathcal{A}_{k-1}`$ produced by the preceding phase as input and
produces a new artifact set $`\mathcal{A}_{k}`$ according to:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       \mathcal{A}_{k}=\Phi_{k}(\mathcal{A}_{k-1},\mathcal{C}_{k})
       ```                                                          |     | (1) |

where $`\mathcal{C}_{k}`$ denotes the task context at phase $`p_{k}`$,
including the task type, run state, and any phase-specific configuration
inherited from earlier phases. Concretely, running $`\Phi_{k}`$ executes
each constituent skill sequentially.

For each skill $`\phi\in\Phi_{k}`$, the Executor selects the appropriate
Python template $`\tau_{k}\in\phi`$ based on the task context
$`\mathcal{C}_{k}`$. Where the template covers the required
configuration, it is executed directly with task-specific parameters
substituted; where adaptation is required, the Executor invokes
Codex \[[35](#bib.bib34)\] as an MCP tool \[[44](#bib.bib46)\], passing
the template and task context to generate a task-specific adaptation.
The Executor then executes the adapted script and verifies it against
the self-validation criteria $`v_{k}`$ specified in the skill’s
Markdown, catching any runtime errors or tracebacks and re-invoking
Codex with the error context to iteratively refine the adaptation until
the script executes successfully. The Executor returns
$`\mathcal{A}_{k}`$ to the Orchestrator only when
$`v_{k}(\mathcal{A}_{k})=1`$, establishing self-validation as a
necessary correctness condition that prevents structurally invalid
outputs from reaching the phase-level validation gate and incurring
unnecessary recovery overhead.

#### III-C2 Validation Gates and Recovery

Each gate verifies that the phase has produced the artifacts the next
phase depends on: a formatted dataset and fingerprint in Task
Understanding, an experiment plan and preprocessed data in Planning, the
optimised configuration and trained weights in Training, and the
aggregated metrics and exported pipeline in Post-Train Processing. At
every phase, the Orchestrator applies the same three categories of
check: structural (expected artifacts and formats), execution (process
completion and exit status), and semantic (task-appropriateness of the
artifacts). What differs between phases is not the checks but the
reference they are evaluated against, which specifies the outputs a
given phase should produce and remains largely stable across runs.

Structural and execution checks are performed programmatically, matching
the produced artifacts against concrete expectations: the files that
must exist, their formats and attributes, and each step’s exit
conditions. The semantic category admits no fixed rule: whether an
artifact suits the task is a matter of convention, so the Orchestrator,
as an LLM, evaluates it against the domain knowledge encoded in the
phase’s reference, for example applying clipping to CT rather than the
z-score normalisation appropriate to MRI.

Formally, the gate evaluates the phase output $`\mathcal{A}_{k}`$
against the phase’s criteria
$`\Gamma_{k}=\Gamma_{k}^{\mathrm{str}}\cup\Gamma_{k}^{\mathrm{exe}}\cup\Gamma_{k}^{\mathrm{sem}}`$,
collecting the structural, execution, and semantic criteria, and passes
only if all are satisfied,

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
g_{k}(\mathcal{A}_{k})=\bigwedge_{\gamma\in\Gamma_{k}}\mathbb{1}_{\gamma}(\mathcal{A}_{k})\;\rightarrow\;\{0,1\}\times\mathcal{L}_{k},
``` |  | (2) |

where $`\mathbb{1}_{\gamma}(\mathcal{A}_{k})=1`$ if $`\mathcal{A}_{k}`$
satisfies criterion $`\gamma`$ and $`0`$ otherwise. For each failed
criterion, the Orchestrator records its category $`c_{i}`$ and a
natural-language summary $`s_{i}`$, producing the structured log

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{k}=\{(c_{i},s_{i})\mid\mathbb{1}_{\gamma_{i}}(\mathcal{A}_{k})=0\},
``` |  | (3) |

returned to the Executor as $`\mathcal{F}_{k}=(0,\mathcal{L}_{k})`$ for
targeted recovery rather than full re-execution. A phase advances only
when its gate passes; it retries while $`r_{k}<R_{\max}`$. If the retry
limit is reached, the Orchestrator invokes a minimal-safe fallback that
performs only the essential operations required by the phase contract
without further optimisation. The fallback is evaluated by the same
gate, and the workflow terminates if it also fails. In our experiments,
normal recovery always succeeded before this fallback was required.
Because each phase executes only on artifacts that have passed all
upstream gates, error propagation is structurally precluded, and every
committed artifact is auditable through the criteria it satisfied.

![Refer to caption](2611.04180v1/gate.png)

Fig. 2: An example validation-gated recovery cycle in the Planning
phase.

Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Fig. 2 ‣ III-C2 Validation Gates and Recovery ‣ III-C Validation-Gated Pipeline Execution ‣ III Methodology ‣ Validation-Gated ML Pipeline Synthesis with Expert-Grounded Self-Evolving Skills")
illustrates an example cycle of this gating-recovery mechanism in the
Planning phase. Taking the formatted dataset and the extracted
fingerprint $`\mathcal{A}_{1}`$ as input, the Orchestrator invokes the
Executor with the Planning skills. The Executor runs the experiment
planning and preprocessing skills and self-validates that the scripts
execute successfully, producing the experiment plan and preprocessed
data as $`\mathcal{A}_{2}`$. The Orchestrator then evaluates
$`\mathcal{A}_{2}`$ at the validation gate: although the structural and
execution checks pass, the semantic check detects that a CT dataset has
been normalised with an MRI-style Z-score rather than the required
clipping, a correctness error that script-level self-validation cannot
catch. The resulting failure context is returned to the Executor for a
targeted retry, and only once all checks pass does the phase advance to
Training.

### III-D Post-Run Skill Evolution

While the Orchestrator’s recovery resolves failures within a run, its
effects are yet transient: the adapted scripts it yields are not
retained, and the guidance that misjudged the case remains unrefined. A
skill encountering a similar condition must therefore rediscover the
same resolution through retries, a pattern that recurs whenever such
conditions arise. The Curator addresses this by operating post-run,
transforming accumulated execution evidence into durable refinements of
the skill library. In-run recovery and post-run evolution are therefore
driven by a common signal: the validation and retry traces emitted at
each gate. The harness persists these traces during execution, so the
Curator’s evolution draws on the same auditable evidence that governs
in-run control.

#### III-D1 Evidence Aggregation and Brittleness Identification

After a run concludes, the Curator aggregates the traces that the
harness persisted for each phase into a per-skill evidence record. For a
skill $`\phi`$, this record collects the retry count it incurred, the
validation logs of the checks it failed, and the adapted script
$`\tau_{\phi}^{\star}`$ that the Executor produced to resolve the
difficult case during recovery:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{E}_{\phi}=\left(r_{\phi},\ \{\mathcal{L}_{k}\mid\phi\in\Phi_{k}\},\ \tau_{\phi}^{\star}\right),\qquad r_{\phi}=\sum_{k:\,\phi\in\Phi_{k}}r_{k}.
``` |  | (4) |

Each skill is first screened by its accumulated retry count
$`r_{\phi}`$, which indicates where the standing guidance may not
sufficiently cover the encountered task conditions. The skill with the
highest retry count is selected for further inspection:

|     |                                       |     |     |
|-----|---------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \phi^{\star}=\arg\max_{\phi}r_{\phi}.
       ```                                    |     | (5) |

The Curator then analyses its complete evidence record, including failed
validation conditions, the recovery sequence, and the successfully
adapted script, to identify the underlying deficiency and determine
whether and how the skill should be updated.

![Refer to caption](2611.04180v1/evolution.png)

Fig. 3: The Curator’s post-run skill evolution loop after a 3D
reconstruction task with HDF5 dataset format.

As shown in
Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Fig. 3 ‣ III-D1 Evidence Aggregation and Brittleness Identification ‣ III-D Post-Run Skill Evolution ‣ III Methodology ‣ Validation-Gated ML Pipeline Synthesis with Expert-Grounded Self-Evolving Skills"),
a 3D reconstruction dataset supplied in HDF5 format forces the Dataset
preparation skill into repeated recovery, as the Executor initially
assumes the NIfTI layout used for segmentation and adapts a new HDF5
preparation script only after retrying. The Curator aggregates the
traces of this run into the skill’s evidence record
$`\mathcal{E}_{\phi}`$, capturing its elevated retry count, the
validation logs of the failed format checks, and the adapted HDF5 script
that ultimately succeeded. Brittleness identification across all skills
then identifies Dataset preparation as the brittleness maximiser
$`\phi^{\star}`$, marking it as the candidate for patching.

#### III-D2 Patch Proposal and Validation

For the flagged skill $`\phi^{\star}`$, the Curator analyses its
evidence record $`\mathcal{E}_{\phi^{\star}}`$ to diagnose the
deficiency underlying the retries, and proposes a patch $`\delta`$
comprising two complementary parts. 1) The adapted script
$`\tau_{\phi^{\star}}^{\star}`$ that the Executor produced to resolve
the difficult case during the run, recorded in the evidence but not yet
part of the library, is consolidated into the skill as a new reusable
template; and 2) the skill’s durable knowledge, its Markdown
specification or reference document, is extended to describe the
condition and when that template applies. Consolidating both the
recovered script and the guidance that selects it transfers the handling
of the condition from reactive recovery to proactive capability,
generalising it to subsequent encounters rather than remedying only the
instance that elicited it.

Before it is committed, the patch is validated by re-executing the
affected step on the precise input $`\mathcal{A}^{\star}`$ that
triggered the retries, and is accepted only if the re-execution
satisfies the corresponding gate:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\phi^{\star}\leftarrow\begin{cases}\phi^{\star}\cup\delta&\text{if }g(\Phi(\mathcal{A}^{\star};\,\phi^{\star}\cup\delta))=1\\
\phi^{\star}&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}
``` |  | (6) |

Validation requires the patched skill to pass the gate on its first
execution without retries, indicating that the guidance now covers the
condition rather than leaving it to reactive recovery. A verified patch
is committed additively, as $`\phi^{\star}\cup\delta`$, extending the
skill while preserving previously covered cases, so evolution maintains
coverage monotonically. Over successive runs, the library thus covers
more of the encountered task distribution.

Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Fig. 3 ‣ III-D1 Evidence Aggregation and Brittleness Identification ‣ III-D Post-Run Skill Evolution ‣ III Methodology ‣ Validation-Gated ML Pipeline Synthesis with Expert-Grounded Self-Evolving Skills")
depicts a representative instance for the Dataset preparation skill: the
Curator consolidates the recovered HDF5 preparation script into the
skill’s templates and extends its specification with a data-type routing
clause that recognises HDF5 inputs up front, then validates the patch by
re-executing preparation on the same dataset. Upon passing the gate, the
patch is committed to the evolved skill library so that the recovered
handling is applied proactively thereafter.

## IV Evaluation

We evaluate the proposed framework through a series of experiments
designed to assess its end-to-end effectiveness, the contribution of its
core design components, and its generalisability. Specifically, we
investigate the following research questions:

RQ1: How does EvoML compare against existing agentic AutoML systems and
command-line coding tools on end-to-end ML pipeline synthesis?
RQ2: To what extent does validation-gated execution contribute to
pipeline automation and model performance?
RQ3: How do expert grounding and post-run skill evolution contribute to
pipeline synthesis performance?
RQ4: How well does the framework generalise beyond the targeted
benchmarks to broader ML tasks?

These RQs follow the design of EvoML and progressively examine its
effectiveness. RQ1 evaluates the complete framework against existing
agentic AutoML systems and coding tools. RQ2 isolates the contribution
of validation-gated execution, while RQ3 examines the effects of expert
grounding and post-run skill evolution. RQ4 then evaluates whether the
framework extends beyond the primary medical-imaging setting to broader
ML tasks.

### IV-A Benchmarking Datasets

We evaluate primarily on medical imaging, a demanding testbed for ML
pipeline synthesis. Existing ML-engineering benchmarks such as
MLE-bench \[[45](#bib.bib60)\] centre on competition-style tasks in
which the challenge is maximising performance through model selection
and tuning, rather than constructing a correct pipeline. Medical imaging
instead combines heterogeneous formats, 2D and 3D volumes, and heavy
modality-specific preprocessing, all under strict correctness
constraints, yet a runnable pipeline can still be silently wrong. We
select eight medical datasets spanning six task types:
BTCV \[[46](#bib.bib49)\]: supervised 3D segmentation of 13 organs in CT
(50 cases; $`512\times 512\times 123`$), with few, imbalanced samples.
ACDC \[[47](#bib.bib48)\]: supervised 3D cardiac segmentation in MRI
($`215\times 228\times 10`$), with pronounced voxel anisotropy.
FLARE21 \[[48](#bib.bib50)\]: supervised 3D segmentation of 4 abdominal
organs in CT (361 cases; $`512\times 512\times 126`$).
FLARE22 \[[49](#bib.bib47)\]: semi-supervised 3D segmentation of 13
abdominal organs in CT (50 labelled, 2000 unlabelled;
$`512\times 512\times 196`$), where label scarcity and semi-supervised
training policy are the central difficulty.
Promise12MSBench \[[50](#bib.bib51)\]: supervised 2D binary prostate
segmentation in MRI ($`512\times 512`$), adapted from
PROMISE12 \[[51](#bib.bib52)\]. OrganMNIST3D \[[52](#bib.bib53)\]:
supervised 3D classification of 11 organ categories in CT (1,742
samples; $`64\times 64\times 64`$), the least demanding task.
FastMRI \[[53](#bib.bib54)\]: supervised 3D reconstruction from
undersampled k-space (60 cases; $`288\times 640\times 16\times 83`$),
demanding for its large HDF5 footprint and k-space pairing.
IXI \[[54](#bib.bib55)\]: supervised 3D denoising of brain MRI (581 T1
volumes; $`256\times 256\times 150`$), requiring fine structure to be
retained while suppressing noise.

### IV-B Evaluation Metrics

We evaluate each system along two dimensions: its ability to
autonomously construct an executable end-to-end ML pipeline, and the
predictive quality of the resulting model. Accordingly, we report
*End-to-End Automation Capability (EAC)* and *Final Model Quality
(FMQ)*.

End-to-End Automation Capability (EAC). EAC measures how autonomously a
method produces a complete, executable pipeline, penalised per step by
the human effort required. We track five milestones: (1) dataset
preparation, (2) model design, (3) training, (4) hyperparameter
optimisation, and (5) pipeline integration. For milestone $`k`$ in run
$`r`$, let $`c_{r,k}\in\{0,1\}`$ indicate completion with a valid
artifact, and $`h_{r,k}`$ the number of interventions at that milestone.
The per-milestone score is:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
s_{r,k}=c_{r,k}\cdot\left(1-\min\!\left(\frac{h_{r,k}}{3},\,1\right)\right),
``` |  | (7) |

where the intervention budget of three distinguishes minor recoverable
failures from cases requiring substantial manual guidance. EAC is the
mean across milestones:

|     |                                                    |     |     |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mathrm{EAC}_{r}=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{k=1}^{5}s_{r,k}.
       ```                                                 |     | (8) |

Each milestone contributes only when completed with a valid artifact,
and its contribution decreases with the number of interventions it
required.

Final Model Quality (FMQ). FMQ measures the predictive performance of
the final model. For segmentation datasets, given predicted foreground
mask $`\hat{Y}_{r,i}`$ and ground-truth mask $`Y_{i}`$ for test case
$`i\in T`$, we use the Dice score \[[55](#bib.bib11),
[56](#bib.bib12)\]:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{FMQ}_{\mathrm{seg},r}=\mathrm{Dice}_{r}=\frac{1}{|T|}\sum_{i\in T}\frac{2|\hat{Y}_{r,i}\cap Y_{i}|}{|\hat{Y}_{r,i}|+|Y_{i}|}.
``` |  | (9) |

For classification datasets, we use accuracy:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{FMQ}_{\mathrm{cls},r}=\mathrm{Acc}_{r}=\frac{1}{|T|}\sum_{i\in T}\mathbb{I}\!\left(\hat{y}_{r,i}=y_{i}\right),
``` |  | (10) |

where $`\hat{y}_{r,i}`$ and $`y_{i}`$ denote the predicted and
ground-truth labels, respectively.

For the reconstruction task, we use the Structural Similarity Index
Measure (SSIM) \[[57](#bib.bib42)\]:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{FMQ}_{\mathrm{rec},r}=\mathrm{SSIM}_{r}=\frac{1}{|T|}\sum_{i\in T}\frac{(2\mu_{p}\mu_{q}+c_{1})(2\sigma_{pq}+c_{2})}{(\mu_{p}^{2}+\mu_{q}^{2}+c_{1})(\sigma_{p}^{2}+\sigma_{q}^{2}+c_{2})},
``` |  | (11) |

where $`p=\hat{Y}_{r,i}`$, $`q=Y_{i}`$, $`\mu_{p}`$, $`\mu_{q}`$ and
$`\sigma_{p}^{2}`$, $`\sigma_{q}^{2}`$ denote the local means and
variances, $`\sigma_{pq}`$ the local covariance, and $`c_{1}`$,
$`c_{2}`$ are numerical stability constants.

For denoising, we use the Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR):

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{FMQ}_{\mathrm{den},r}=\mathrm{PSNR}_{r}=\frac{1}{|T|}\sum_{i\in T}10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{L^{2}}{\mathrm{MSE}(\hat{Y}_{r,i},\,Y_{i})}\right),
``` |  | (12) |

where $`L`$ is the maximum possible pixel intensity value and
$`\mathrm{MSE}(\hat{Y}_{r,i},Y_{i})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}(\hat{Y}_{r,i,j}-Y_{i,j})^{2}`$.

### IV-C Experiment Settings

#### IV-C1 Baseline Selection and Configuration

We compare against two categories of baselines: three agentic AutoML
systems targeting end-to-end ML pipeline construction,
AutoML-Agent \[[17](#bib.bib1)\], MLZero \[[18](#bib.bib2)\], and
M3Builder \[[19](#bib.bib29)\]; and two widely adopted command-line
coding tools, Codex \[[35](#bib.bib34)\] (GPT-5.5 Medium) and Claude
Code \[[36](#bib.bib35)\] (Opus 4.7 Medium). To ensure a fair
comparison, we apply the same task requirements to all baselines. For
the agentic AutoML systems, we preserve each system’s native prompting
conventions so that it operates under the input format for which it was
designed, and additionally supply the skeleton and template files that
certain baselines require, following the setup specified in their
respective implementations. For the command-line coding tools, we
provide the same task description as EvoML and guide them through the
same four-phase workflow, ensuring that all methods address an
equivalent synthesis task.

#### IV-C2 Environment and Protocol

All experiments are conducted on an Ubuntu 22.04 server equipped with an
AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3995WX CPU (64 cores), 252GB of RAM, and two
NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs (48GB VRAM each). We provide all methods in a
unified Python environment pre-installed with ML and medical imaging
libraries and common dependencies, and each method may install
additional dependencies as needed during pipeline execution to ensure a
fair comparison. To account for the stochasticity of LLM-based
generation, each method is executed three times per dataset, and we
report the mean $`\pm`$ std of EAC and FMQ.

### IV-D Experiment Results

#### IV-D1 Comparison with Baseline Methods

Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Fig. 4 ‣ IV-C2 Environment and Protocol ‣ IV-C Experiment Settings ‣ IV Evaluation ‣ Validation-Gated ML Pipeline Synthesis with Expert-Grounded Self-Evolving Skills")
compares EvoML against the five baselines across the eight datasets. On
automation (EAC), EvoML is the only method that reaches $`1.0`$ on every
dataset, as its validation-gated harness resolves stage failures within
the retry budget without human intervention. The baselines reflect their
design assumptions. M3Builder handles supervised 3D segmentation
reliably but falls short on the semi-supervised and non-segmentation
tasks, where its EAC drops to $`0.4667`$ on FLARE22 and FastMRI. MLZero,
relying on documentation retrieval and iterative trial rather than a
fixed workflow, completes pipelines unevenly ($`0.5111`$ to $`0.7778`$)
as its exploratory loops stall on harder tasks. AutoML-Agent, lifted by
the code skeleton we supply, reaches near $`1.0`$ on the easier
segmentation and classification tasks but fails to adapt to harder
scenarios, dropping to $`0.7778`$ on BTCV and $`0.7555`$ on IXI. The
command-line tools are the most autonomous baselines, recovering from
runtime errors by monitoring the terminal, yet they require intervention
on the reconstruction and denoising tasks, where failures arise from
modelling design rather than execution.

On model performance (FMQ), EvoML attains the best result on every
dataset, owing to its expert-grounded skills and the systematic HPO and
promotion the baselines lack. The margin is largest on the harder tasks,
reaching $`0.9498`$ on FastMRI against the next-best $`0.8579`$ and
$`0.7859`$ on IXI against $`0.7215`$. The baselines degrade in ways that
trace to their design: the command-line tools stay competitive on easier
tasks but fall away on the hardest, with Codex dropping to $`0.6167`$ on
BTCV and $`0.5309`$ on IXI, while the dedicated AutoML systems collapse
more sharply, AutoML-Agent to $`0.3837`$ on ACDC and M3Builder to
$`0.1979`$ on FastMRI.

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| Method |  Input Pairing |  Model |  Loss / Output | FMQ |
| Codex |  Synthesised from target |  U-Net3D |  L1+SSIM, 1-ch | 0.8579 |
| Claude Code |  Synthesised from target |  U-Net3D |  L1+SSIM, 1-ch | 0.8521 |
| MLZero |  Backprojection $`\to`$ temptv |  U-Net2D |  L1, 1-ch | 0.6953 |
| AutoML-Agent |  Zero-filled $`\to`$ temptv |  U-Net2D |  SSIM, 4-ch sigmoid | 0.6583 |
| M3Builder |  Zero-filled $`\to`$ temptv |  U-Net3DTiny |  L1+SSIM, 4-ch sigmoid | 0.1979 |
| EvoML |  Undersampled $`\to`$ full k-space RSS |  VarNet3D |  L1+SSIM, 1-ch | 0.9498 |

TABLE I: FastMRI reconstruction pipeline design choices across methods,
with resulting mean FMQ (SSIM).

We take FastMRI as a representative case, since reconstruction exposes
the widest range of quality and allows clear right-and-wrong design
choices.
Table [I](#S4.T1 "TABLE I ‣ IV-D1 Comparison with Baseline Methods ‣ IV-D Experiment Results ‣ IV Evaluation ‣ Validation-Gated ML Pipeline Synthesis with Expert-Grounded Self-Evolving Skills")
compares each method’s input–target pairing strategy, model design, and
loss function selection, and the results track how faithfully each
handles the reconstruction-specific requirements. The command-line tools
adopt a sound model and loss function but shortcut the data pairing,
synthesising the input from the target rather than the measured k-space,
which simplifies the task and yields competitive but lower SSIM. MLZero
makes sounder choices, reconstructing via backprojection with an
L1-trained 2D U-Net. AutoML-Agent and M³Builder fare the worst,
importing segmentation defaults unsuited to reconstruction: both pair a
coarsely resized, zero-filled reconstruction with a mismatched target
and retain a multi-channel sigmoid output suited to label maps rather
than intensity regression, with M³Builder collapsing to $`0.1979`$ under
the most aggressive resizing. EvoML follows the correct protocol,
undersampling the fully sampled k-space relative to the full RSS target,
using a reconstruction-specific VarNet3D and an L1–SSIM objective,
achieving the highest FMQ. Final quality thus depends less on model
capacity than on whether the pipeline respects the task structure, which
is what EvoML’s expert grounding enforces.

EvoML is also markedly more consistent, with FMQ standard deviation
below $`0.013`$ on every dataset, whereas the baselines fluctuate widely
(AutoML-Agent $`\pm 0.2127`$ on IXI, M3Builder $`\pm 0.1317`$ on
FLARE22). This stability stems from the expert-grounded skills, which
anchor every run in the same proven nnU-Net procedure rather than
re-deriving the pipeline, while evolution reinforces it by settling the
correct task-specific handling into the skills so quality-determining
choices are applied reliably across runs.

#### IV-D2 Ablation Study

We conduct two ablations to isolate the contributions of EvoML’s core
components: the validation-gated execution harness and the
expert-grounded, self-evolving skill design. Each ablation removes or
varies one component while holding the rest of the framework fixed, and
is evaluated under the same protocol as the main comparison.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Fig. 5: Effect of validation gating: without gates, EAC and FMQ both
decline, sharply on the harder reconstruction, denoising, and
semi-supervised tasks.

Validation Gating. To isolate the contribution of validation-gated
execution, we compare full EvoML against a variant in which the gates
are removed, so stages progress unconditionally and failures are neither
detected nor automatically recovered.
Figure [5](#S4.F5 "Fig. 5 ‣ IV-D2 Ablation Study ‣ IV-D Experiment Results ‣ IV Evaluation ‣ Validation-Gated ML Pipeline Synthesis with Expert-Grounded Self-Evolving Skills")
reports both metrics across the eight datasets. The removal of
validation gates degrades automation wherever failures arise: a faulty
artifact can no longer be detected and repaired in place, so pipeline
completion reverts to manual intervention, and EAC declines from $`1.0`$
to as low as $`0.5333`$ on IXI and $`0.6000`$ on FastMRI. This
degradation scales with task difficulty, leaving the simpler OrganMNIST,
FLARE21, and ACDC largely unaffected while the more demanding
reconstruction, denoising, and semi-supervised tasks deteriorate
substantially. Model quality declines in parallel, though for a more
subtle reason. The errors intercepted by the gates are frequently not
outright failures but silent inconsistencies, such as the application of
an MRI-style normalisation to CT data, which execute without error yet
corrupt the training process. Left unchecked, such errors propagate into
the model and manifest only as degraded output: FMQ falls most markedly
on the hardest tasks, declining from $`0.9199`$ to $`0.7422`$ on FLARE22
and from $`0.9498`$ to $`0.7116`$ on FastMRI, while the simplest task,
OrganMNIST, remains nearly unaffected. The gates thus safeguard both
autonomy, by recovering failures automatically, and quality, by
arresting silent errors before they reach the model.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Skill Expert-Grounding and Evolution. We examine the skill design along
two axes: the contribution of expert grounding, and the contribution of
post-run evolution.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Fig. 6: Effect of expert grounding: without the nnU-Net grounding, both
automation and quality fall and variance roughly doubles.

Expert-Grounding. We compare full EvoML against a variant that keeps the
skill structure, harness, and evolution but removes the nnU-Net
grounding, replacing dataset preparation, fingerprinting, planning,
preprocessing, training, and evaluation with generic, executor-designed
equivalents. Lacking a proven procedure to follow, the executor
re-derives each step from scratch, so its choices vary from run to run
and often miss the dataset-specific handling the grounded skills encode.
As
Figure [6](#S4.F6 "Fig. 6 ‣ IV-D2 Ablation Study ‣ IV-D Experiment Results ‣ IV Evaluation ‣ Validation-Gated ML Pipeline Synthesis with Expert-Grounded Self-Evolving Skills")
shows, these ad hoc steps fail more often, lowering EAC to as low as
$`0.6667`$ on FLARE22, and yield weaker models, with FMQ dropping from
$`0.9199`$ to $`0.7150`$ on FLARE22 and $`0.9498`$ to $`0.7967`$ on
FastMRI; run-to-run variance also roughly doubles, since each run
reconstructs the pipeline independently. Expert grounding therefore
raises quality, sustains autonomy, and reduces variance.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

(a) Synthesis time

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

(b) Token consumption

Fig. 7: Effect of post-run evolution: evolution reduces synthesis time
and token consumption across the dataset sequence.

Skill Evolution. We isolate post-run evolution by disabling the Curator:
the Executor still adapts templates online, but neither the adapted
scripts nor the guidance refinements are retained, so every dataset runs
against the original library. Both configurations run over an identical,
fixed dataset order, from segmentation (BTCV, ACDC, FLARE21, the
semi-supervised FLARE22, Promise12) through classification (OrganMNIST)
to the hardest reconstruction and denoising tasks (FastMRI, IXI). Only
the evolving configuration accumulates experience across this sequence.
Results are shown in
Figure [7](#S4.F7 "Fig. 7 ‣ IV-D2 Ablation Study ‣ IV-D Experiment Results ‣ IV Evaluation ‣ Validation-Gated ML Pipeline Synthesis with Expert-Grounded Self-Evolving Skills").
Evolution reduces total synthesis time by roughly 41% (from 490 to 290
minutes) and token consumption by roughly 30% (from 71 to 50 million),
as later datasets can reuse previously recovered scripts and guidance
instead of rediscovering them through repeated adaptation. Beyond
efficiency, we assess evolution using three process-level criteria:
first-pass skill success, whether a skill completes without recovery;
validation-triggered retries, the number of recovery attempts caused by
failed gates; and cross-task reuse, whether adaptations retained from
earlier datasets improve first-pass execution on later tasks. Excluding
BTCV, where no prior evolution is available, first-pass skill success
increases from 36/63 (57.1%) to 50/63 (79.4%), while
validation-triggered retries decrease from 27 to 13 ($`-51.9\%`$).
Cross-task reuse is also visible on later datasets: Promise12 and
OrganMNIST complete all nine skill executions on the first pass, while
IXI improves from 3/9 to 9/9 after accumulated evolution. The two
configurations coincide on BTCV, confirming that these gains arise only
after experience has accumulated across runs. These process-level
criteria complement FMQ by capturing changes in execution behaviour
across runs, allowing us to distinguish retained procedural improvement
from changes in final predictive performance.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### IV-E Generalisation

To test whether EvoML generalises beyond nnU-Net’s medical grounding
domain, we evaluate it on three general ML tasks: natural image
classification (CIFAR-10 \[[58](#bib.bib56)\]), natural image
segmentation (VOC2012 \[[59](#bib.bib57)\]), and text classification (AG
News \[[60](#bib.bib58)\]), against all five baselines. These general
tasks are comparatively simple and follow well-established pipelines, so
all methods achieve near-perfect automation, with EAC close to $`1.0`$
throughout;
Table [II](#S4.T2 "TABLE II ‣ IV-E Generalisation ‣ IV Evaluation ‣ Validation-Gated ML Pipeline Synthesis with Expert-Grounded Self-Evolving Skills")
therefore reports FMQ, the dimension on which they differ.

| Method       | CIFAR-10             | VOC2012              | AG News              |

| AutoML-Agent | 0.9419 $`\pm`$0.0027 | 0.7328 $`\pm`$0.0084 | 0.9103 $`\pm`$0.0056 |
| MLZero       | 0.9466 $`\pm`$0.0030 | 0.7117 $`\pm`$0.0068 | 0.9441 $`\pm`$0.0033 |
| Codex        | 0.9424 $`\pm`$0.0042 | 0.7036 $`\pm`$0.0088 | 0.9207 $`\pm`$0.0061 |
| Claude Code  | 0.9391 $`\pm`$0.0032 | 0.7086 $`\pm`$0.0065 | 0.9457 $`\pm`$0.0039 |

TABLE II: Generalisation to three general ML tasks: FMQ (mean $`\pm`$
std).

EvoML achieves the best FMQ across all three tasks, confirming that its
framework generalises beyond medical imaging. The expert-grounded skills
are not rigidly tied to the medical setting: the Executor adapts them to
each new domain and post-run evolution refines them further, so the
grounded procedures continue to benefit general tasks. The margins are
narrower here than on the medical benchmarks largely because these tasks
are simpler and more standardised, leaving less room to distinguish
methods, yet EvoML’s combination of adapted expert skills,
validation-gated execution, and evolution still yields the strongest
results on every task.

### V-A Architectural Comparison with Baselines

| Method |     Manual-Artifact-  Free Input |     Expert  Grounding |     Stage-Gated  Validation |     Cross-run  Evolution |
| M³Builder |     ✗  (DataCard required) |     ✓  (Fixed templates) |     ✗  (Shallow output check) | ✗ |
| AutoML-Agent |     ✗  (Skeleton required) | ✗ |     ✗  (Validation on  pseudo execution) | ✗ |
| MLZero | ✓ |     ✗  (Document retrieval) |     ✗  (Execution only) | ✗ |
| Codex | ✓ | ✗ |     ✗  (Execution only) | ✗ |

TABLE III: Architectural comparison of EvoML against agentic AutoML
systems and command-line coding tools.

Table [III](#S5.T3 "TABLE III ‣ V-A Architectural Comparison with Baselines ‣ V Discussion ‣ Validation-Gated ML Pipeline Synthesis with Expert-Grounded Self-Evolving Skills")
contrasts EvoML with the baselines on the architectural dimension that
distinguishes it. M3Builder and AutoML-Agent require a user-supplied
skeleton or templates, whereas MLZero and the command-line tools run
from minimal input but lack expert grounding. On validation, the
baselines check only execution success (MLZero, command-line tools),
file and shape structure (M3Builder), or conformance to user
requirements assessed over pseudo-execution rather than real runs
(AutoML-Agent); none verify task-level correctness, so a runnable but
task-inappropriate pipeline passes unflagged. Furthermore, no baselines
retain experience once a run completes. EvoML alone combines
minimal-input operation, adaptive expert grounding, task-aware
validation, and cross-run evolution, the combination that yields its
automation, quality, and consistency.

TABLE IV: Cost-efficiency comparison against expert leaderboard

We compare EvoML against expert-engineered leaderboard solutions for the
evaluated datasets. As shown in
Table [IV](#S5.T4 "TABLE IV ‣ V-B Cost Against Human Expert Development ‣ V Discussion ‣ Validation-Gated ML Pipeline Synthesis with Expert-Grounded Self-Evolving Skills"),
EvoML surpasses the expert reference on FLARE21, FLARE22, and Promise12,
remains close on OrganMNIST3D and FastMRI, but performs lower on ACDC
and BTCV. Overall, EvoML achieves competitive model quality while
substantially reducing synthesis effort and cost. The comparison
underscores EvoML’s cost-efficiency: developing a leaderboard-level
solution typically requires on the order of 8 to 40 hours of expert
effort depending on task difficulty, excluding unattended model
training, corresponding to roughly \$800 to \$6,000 in labour cost,
whereas EvoML synthesises a pipeline in about 20–45 minutes at a
generation cost of \$10 to \$35. It thus trades expensive, scarce expert
time for cheap, fully automated synthesis while remaining competitive in
quality.

### V-C Threats to Validity

1. Internal validity: EvoML depends on the underlying foundation model.
To assess this effect, we rerun the full framework with Claude Opus 4.7
on BTCV, FLARE22, and FastMRI. The resulting FMQ differs from GPT-5.5 by
less than 0.008, suggesting that the main findings are not specific to
one backbone. Since Opus 4.7 costs roughly 1.7× as much per pipeline, we
use GPT-5.5 as the default backbone for comparable quality at a lower
synthesis cost. 2. Construct validity: EvoML incurs longer
model-training time because its nnU-Net grounding includes thorough
preprocessing, augmentation, and five-fold cross-validation. On a
typical supervised segmentation task, the baselines train in roughly 10
hours, EvoML in 60, and nnU-Net in 300. We consider this additional
computation a trade-off for the stronger automation and model quality
enabled by the grounded workflow. 3. External validity: We focus
primarily on medical imaging because its pipelines rely on
domain-specific processing and modelling choices, where mistakes can
remain executable yet still degrade final model quality. We additionally
evaluate three general ML tasks as initial evidence beyond this setting.
For broader SE tasks, the same principles remain applicable: workflows
can be decomposed into stages, recurring procedures can be encoded as
skills, intermediate artifacts can be validated before downstream
execution, and successful recoveries can be retained across tasks.
Extending EvoML therefore mainly requires adapting the skill content and
validation criteria.

## VI Conclusion

We presented EvoML, an agentic framework for end-to-end ML pipeline
synthesis built on expert-grounded skills, validation-gated execution,
and post-run skill evolution. By advancing each phase only when its
outputs satisfy structural, execution, and semantic checks, EvoML limits
error propagation, while post-run evolution consolidates successful
recoveries into persistent skill updates that improve execution across
subsequent tasks. Across eight medical-imaging datasets and three
general ML tasks, EvoML achieved full automation and the strongest, most
consistent model quality among the compared systems, while substantially
reducing synthesis effort relative to expert development. Our additional
evolution analysis further shows improved first-pass skill success,
fewer validation-triggered retries, and cross-task reuse of retained
adaptations. Future work will extend EvoML to broader ML and
software-engineering tasks and investigate finer-grained validation
throughout the pipeline to further improve model quality and
reliability.

available at:
